title: Virtual Machines (Basic)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Decide when an IaaS virtual machine is the right tool for a workload, and what you still manage yourself.
- Name every resource Azure creates for a VM — image, size, disks, network interface, virtual network, public IP and network security group — and explain what each one does.
- Choose a VM size family and a managed disk type, including when a burstable B-series size is a good fit.
- Compare the ways to sign in to and connect to a VM, and explain why new virtual networks need explicit outbound access.
- Explain power states and billing, resizing, auto-shutdown and the main VM pricing options.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Monday, 08:15. The storefront server next to the pantry is humming loudly again, and Pak Budi has placed a desk fan in front of it "just for today". Ibu Sari has read your cloud-concepts notes from Lunch 02 and has a simple request: "Before we redesign anything, can we at least get the shop off that box and into Azure?"

Dewi is excited. "It's only Ubuntu and nginx. Give me a server in the cloud and I'll copy the site over this afternoon." Pak Budi is less excited. He wants to know who can sign in, which ports will be open to the internet, and whether the new server can still download security updates. Then the finance team asks the question everyone was avoiding: "Will we keep paying for it at night, when nobody is shopping?"

Your job today is to rent that first server properly. What exactly do you get — and pay for — when you create a virtual machine in Azure?

Reading

1. When a virtual machine is the right tool

A virtual machine (VM) is a computer that Azure runs for you on its own physical servers. You choose an operating system image and a size, Azure finds a host with free capacity, and a few minutes later you have a machine you can sign in to. It is the purest form of infrastructure as a service (IaaS): Microsoft owns the buildings, the physical hosts, the hypervisor and the physical network; you own everything from the operating system upwards — patches, the firewall inside the OS, the web server, the application and its data. In the shared-responsibility picture from Lunch 02, a VM is the cloud option that leaves the most work on your side of the line.

So why pick the option with the most work? Because sometimes control matters more than convenience:

- Lift and shift. The storefront already runs on Ubuntu with nginx. Moving it to a VM — called rehosting — needs almost no code changes, so Nusantara Retail can leave the pantry room this month and modernise later.
- Full control of the operating system. Some software needs a particular kernel module, a vendor agent, or a licence tied to the OS.
- Software that was never built for the cloud. Older business applications that expect a fixed disk path, a Windows service or a fixed hostname are happiest on a VM.
- Short-lived environments. Developers can create, break and delete test servers in minutes.

If all you want is to run a web application, a platform service such as Azure App Service (Lunch 10), a container (Lunch 13) or a function (Lunch 14) usually costs less effort, because Azure patches and scales the platform for you. A good habit: choose a VM when you need control, and write down why. That note will tell you when it is time to modernise.

2. The building blocks: a VM is a bundle of resources

When you select Create in the portal or run az vm create, Azure Resource Manager does not create one thing. It creates a small family of separate resources in your resource group, each with its own resource ID, its own settings and — sometimes — its own line on the bill. Knowing the family is the difference between a tidy subscription and a pile of forgotten disks.

Building block | What it is | Nusantara Retail example | Watch out for
Image | Template for the OS disk, from Azure Marketplace or your own | Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS | Choose a supported, current version
Size | vCPUs, memory, local storage, bandwidth and features | Standard_B2ats_v2 | Not every size exists in every region or zone
OS disk | Managed disk created from the image | 30 GiB holding Ubuntu and nginx | Billed even while the VM is off
Data disk | Extra managed disks you attach, format and mount | 8 GiB for product images | Azure attaches it; you format it
Temporary disk | Local storage on the physical host, if the size has one | None on Basv2 sizes | Wiped when the VM moves host — never keep data there
Network interface (NIC) | Connects the VM to a subnet and holds its private IP | 10.20.1.4 | Every VM needs at least one
Virtual network and subnet | Your private address space in Azure | vnet-nusa-web, 10.20.0.0/16 | Avoid overlap with head office's 10.0.0.0/16
Public IP address | Internet-facing address, Standard SKU | pip-web-1 | Basic SKU was retired on September 30, 2025
Network security group (NSG) | Allow and deny rules for a NIC or subnet | nsg-web | Standard public IPs stay closed until an NSG allows traffic

The image decides what lands on the OS disk. New Generation 2 VMs created from the portal, the CLI or PowerShell now use Trusted Launch by default — Secure Boot plus a virtual TPM that protect the boot process — at no extra cost. Lunch 23 returns to it.

Two practical lessons follow from this table. First, if you let az vm create invent the network, it picks 10.0.0.0/16 — exactly Pak Budi's head-office range. Harmless today, painful on the day you connect the two networks (Lunch 26), so the lab names its own range. Second, deleting a VM does not always delete its disks, NIC and public IP; the portal shows "delete with VM" options, and leftovers keep costing money. In labs, deleting the whole resource group is the clean way out.

3. Choosing a size and a disk

A VM size fixes the number of vCPUs, the memory, any local disk, the maximum number of data disks and the network bandwidth. Size names look cryptic but follow a pattern. In Standard_B2ats_v2, B is the family, 2 is the number of vCPUs, a means an AMD processor (p would mean Arm), t means a tiny amount of memory, s means it can use Premium SSD disks, and v2 is the version of the series. A d in a name means the size has a local temporary disk.

Family | Optimised for | Typical workloads | Nusantara Retail example
B — burstable | Low baseline CPU with short bursts | Small web servers, dev/test, proofs of concept | The first storefront VM
D — general purpose | Balanced CPU and memory | Most production apps, app servers, small databases | A steady inventory API
E — memory optimised | More memory per vCPU | Relational databases, caches, in-memory analytics | A larger SQL Server later
F — compute optimised | More CPU per GiB of memory | Batch jobs, CPU-heavy web tiers, game servers | Nightly price recalculation
L — storage optimised | Large, fast local disks | NoSQL databases, big data, data warehouses | A product-search cluster
M — very large memory | Terabytes of RAM | SAP HANA, very large in-memory databases | Not needed — good to know
N — GPU | NVIDIA or AMD graphics processors | AI training and inference, rendering, graphic workstations | An image-recognition model

Burstable B-series sizes deserve a closer look, because they are cheap and easy to misuse. Each size has a baseline — a share of its vCPUs it can always use. Below the baseline the VM banks CPU credits; above it, the VM spends them. One credit is roughly one vCPU running at 100% for one minute. A Standard_B2ats_v2 has a baseline of 20%, starts with 60 credits, earns up to 24 credits an hour while idle and can bank up to 576. If both vCPUs run flat out, it spends about 1.6 credits per minute, so a brand-new VM can sprint for roughly 35–40 minutes. When the credits run out, Azure throttles it back to the baseline until it earns more. That suits the storefront — mostly quiet, with short peaks — but not a three-hour report that keeps the CPU busy. Watch the CPU Credits Remaining metric. One more note: the original B-series sizes (such as B1s) are End of Life — since July 2026 new subscriptions can't deploy them, and they retire on November 15, 2028 — so new designs use Bsv2, Basv2 or Bpsv2.

Tip: Before you choose, list the sizes your subscription can actually use in a region: az vm list-skus --location southeastasia --size Standard_B --resource-type virtualMachines --output table. The Restrictions column tells you when a size is not offered to you or not available in a zone.

Every VM disk is a managed disk: Azure stores and replicates it for you, and you pick its type.

Disk type | Best for | Can be the OS disk? | Good to know
Standard HDD | Backups, rarely used data | Yes, but retiring for OS disks on September 8, 2028 | Cheapest; latency varies
Standard SSD | Web servers, light apps, dev/test | Yes | A sensible default for small VMs
Premium SSD | Production apps and databases | Yes | Fixed size tiers; needs a size with s in its name
Premium SSD v2 | Databases that need tunable performance | No — data disks only | Set capacity, IOPS and throughput separately
Ultra Disk | The most demanding I/O, such as SAP HANA | No — data disks only | Change performance without restarting the VM

You pay for the provisioned size, rounded up to the next size tier, whether the disk is full or empty. Standard SSD and Premium SSD also come in zone-redundant (ZRS) versions. Disk choice even affects the uptime promise: at the time of writing (October 2026), a single VM whose disks are all Premium SSD or Ultra Disk has a 99.9% connectivity SLA, Standard SSD gives 99.5% and Standard HDD only 95% — check the service level agreements for current figures.

4. Getting in, and getting out

First, authentication — how you prove who you are to the operating system:

- SSH key pairs are the default for Linux. --generate-ssh-keys creates a pair in ~/.ssh; Azure stores only the public key on the VM, and the private key never leaves you.
- Passwords are required for Windows and possible on Linux. Avoid them on Linux; if you must use one, generate it.
- Microsoft Entra ID login lets people sign in with their company identity. Access is granted with Azure RBAC roles such as Virtual Machine User Login or Virtual Machine Administrator Login (Lunch 05). When Rizky's contract ends, you remove a role assignment — no keys to hunt down.

Then, connecting:

- SSH (port 22) for Linux and RDP (port 3389) for Windows need a network path and an NSG rule.
- Azure Bastion is a managed jump host inside your virtual network. You connect from the browser, and the VM needs no public IP at all. The free Developer SKU suits dev/test in selected regions (Southeast Asia is one) and handles one VM at a time; Basic, Standard and Premium are paid SKUs for production.
- Run Command executes a script inside the VM through the Azure VM agent, with no inbound port. The lab uses it to mount a disk.
- Serial console gives you a text console through boot diagnostics, even when networking inside the VM is broken.

Inbound traffic meets the NSG. Its default rules allow traffic from inside the virtual network and from Azure's load balancer probe, then deny everything else — including anything from the internet. For a Linux VM, az vm create also adds a rule that allows SSH from anywhere — convenient for a lab, risky in production, where you would restrict the source address or use Bastion. Web traffic on port 80 stays blocked until you add a rule, for example with az vm open-port. Lunch 08 covers NSGs properly.

Outbound traffic has changed recently, and it surprises people.

Important: Virtual networks created with Azure API versions released after March 31, 2026 — and the portal already does this — use private subnets: VMs get no default outbound internet access. A VM that must reach the internet (for apt-get update, Windows activation or calling an external API) needs an explicit method: a public IP on the VM, a NAT gateway on the subnet, or load balancer outbound rules. Existing virtual networks are not changed.

Today's storefront VM has its own Standard public IP, so it has explicit outbound access and can install nginx. Remove that IP without adding a NAT gateway, and apt-get simply hangs.

5. Living with a VM: power states, billing, resizing and auto-shutdown

A VM moves through power states, and only some of them stop the compute meter.

Power state | What is happening | Compute billed?
Starting | The VM is booting | Yes
Running | Normal working state | Yes
Stopping | The OS is shutting down | Yes
Stopped (allocated) | The OS is off, but the VM still holds its place on the host | Yes
Deallocating | Azure is releasing the host capacity | No
Deallocated | Only the disks and IP addresses remain | No — disks and public IPs are still billed

Warning: Shutting down from inside the operating system (sudo shutdown -h now) or running az vm stop leaves the VM Stopped (allocated) — and still billed for compute. Use the portal's Stop button, az vm deallocate or auto-shutdown, which all deallocate.

Deallocation keeps your managed disks and a Standard public IP keeps its address, because Standard IPs are always static. Anything on the temporary disk is lost, and the next start may land on a different physical host.

Resizing is vertical scaling: you change the size, Azure restarts the VM, and it comes back with more or fewer resources. az vm list-vm-resize-options shows the sizes available on the hardware cluster where your VM runs today. If the size you want is missing, deallocate the VM first so Azure can place it anywhere in the region. When one bigger VM is no longer enough, you scale out instead — more VMs behind a load balancer (Lunch 09) or a scale set (Lunch 23).

Auto-shutdown deallocates a VM at the same time every day and can email you first. The portal lets you choose a time zone; the CLI expects UTC, so 19:00 in Jakarta (UTC+7) is 1200. It is perfect for test VMs and dangerous for anything customers use.

Two ways to configure a VM without logging in will appear throughout the course. cloud-init reads "custom data" on the first boot of a Linux VM to install packages, write files and run commands. VM extensions are small add-ons installed by the Azure VM agent — the Custom Script extension, the Azure Monitor Agent, Microsoft Entra login and many more. Marketplace images already include the agent.

6. Paying for VMs, and what it means for Nusantara Retail

Compute is billed only while a VM is allocated; disks and public IPs are billed while they exist; data leaving Azure and Windows licences add to the bill. Five purchase options change the price of the compute part:

Option | How it works | Good for | Nusantara Retail example
Pay-as-you-go | No commitment; pay for the time the VM is allocated | Labs, tests, new workloads | The first weeks after migration
Reservations | Commit to a VM size in a region for one or three years | Steady servers that won't change | The storefront once its size is settled
Azure savings plan for compute | Commit to an hourly spend for one or three years, across sizes and regions | Steady spend that may change shape | A future mix of VMs and App Service
Spot | Spare capacity at a deep discount; evicted with 30 seconds' notice; no SLA | Interruptible batch jobs, dev/test | Overnight image-thumbnail jobs (Lunch 23)
Azure Hybrid Benefit | Reuse eligible Windows Server or SQL Server licences (also RHEL and SLES subscriptions) | Windows and SQL Server VMs | The back-office Windows server

Lunch 19 turns these into a cost strategy.

Here is the first-step plan for Nusantara Retail. Production will run in Indonesia Central (Jakarta) to keep customer data in the country; the labs use Southeast Asia for the widest service choice. The storefront gets one Ubuntu 24.04 VM on a burstable B2ats_v2 size, because traffic is spiky but mostly low. Its OS disk is Premium SSD for the 99.9% single-VM SLA; product images live on a separate data disk. The NSG allows HTTP and HTTPS from the internet, and SSH only from head office — or nobody at all once Bastion is in place. The VM's public IP gives it the explicit outbound access it needs for updates. Test copies get auto-shutdown and are deallocated at night; the production VM does not.

That answers finance, but not yet the director. A single VM is still a single point of failure: 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month, and planned maintenance or a host failure can restart it. Networking (Lunch 08), load balancing (Lunch 09) and scale sets (Lunch 23) remove that weak spot step by step.

Pause and think: Dewi suggests enabling auto-shutdown at 19:00 WIB on the production storefront VM to save money. What happens to the shoppers who browse after dinner — and which of Nusantara Retail's VMs should get auto-shutdown instead?

Availability sets and zones, scale sets with autoscale, custom images, Spot VMs and patching at scale continue in Lunch 23 · Virtual Machines (Advanced) (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/lunches/23-virtual-machines-advanced.html).

Field notes from Stefanus

The two-in-the-morning question. In design reviews I ask one question about every VM: what state should it be in at two in the morning? If the answer is "off", I want auto-shutdown or a schedule that deallocates it — not a promise, and not a shutdown from inside the operating system, which leaves the compute meter running. If the answer is "gone", I delete the resource group, not just the VM, because orphaned disks and public IP addresses are the quiet line items that survive a hasty cleanup. And if the answer is "busy", I check the size family before anyone touches the code: a burstable VM that has used up its CPU credits looks exactly like a bug.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Virtual machine sizes overview (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-machines/sizes/overview) — every family and series, with the naming rules decoded.
- Microsoft Learn: Azure managed disk types (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-machines/disks-types) — performance limits and when to choose each disk type.
- Microsoft Learn: States and billing status of Azure Virtual Machines (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-machines/states-billing) — the official power-state and billing table.
- Microsoft Learn: Default outbound access in Azure (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-network/ip-services/default-outbound-access) — private subnets and the explicit outbound options.

quiz.q: Dewi finished testing at 18:00 and ran sudo shutdown -h now inside the test VM. Next morning, finance asks why the VM was billed for compute all night. What happened, and what should she do instead?
quiz.a: Shutting down from inside the OS leaves the VM Stopped (allocated), which is still billed for compute. She should deallocate it — the portal's Stop button, az vm deallocate or auto-shutdown — why: only deallocation releases the host capacity that the compute meter charges for.

quiz.q: A nightly sales report keeps both vCPUs of a Standard_B2ats_v2 VM at 100% for three hours. After about 40 minutes it becomes painfully slow. Why, and what would you change?
quiz.a: The VM used up its CPU credits and was throttled to its 20% baseline. Use a non-burstable size such as a D-series (balanced) or F-series (compute optimised) VM for sustained CPU work — why: B-series sizes are designed for workloads that are quiet most of the time and burst only briefly.

quiz.q: Pak Budi creates a new virtual network with the current API, adds a VM without a public IP, and apt-get update hangs. Nothing else is wrong. What is missing?
quiz.a: An explicit outbound method. New virtual networks use private subnets, so the VM needs a NAT gateway on the subnet (the usual choice), load balancer outbound rules, or its own public IP — why: default outbound access is no longer given to VMs in private subnets.

quiz.q: You want the highest single-VM SLA for the production storefront. Which disk types can you use for the OS disk and for the data disk?
quiz.a: A Premium SSD OS disk, with Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 or Ultra Disk data disks — why: the top single-instance SLA (99.9% at the time of writing) requires premium-class storage, and Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk cannot be OS disks.

quiz.q: Rizky, an outsourced contractor, must troubleshoot the storefront VM for one week. Pak Budi does not want port 22 open to the internet or SSH keys handed around. What do you set up?
quiz.a: Azure Bastion (or Run Command for scripted tasks) plus Microsoft Entra ID login, with a Virtual Machine User Login role assignment for Rizky that you remove after the week — why: Bastion needs no public inbound port, and access tied to an identity and an RBAC role is easy to grant and revoke.

takeaways: A VM is IaaS: Azure runs the hardware and hypervisor; you own the OS, patches, software and data.
"One VM" is a bundle of resources — VM, OS disk, data disks, NIC, virtual network, Standard public IP and NSG — and leftovers keep costing money until you delete them.
Pick the size family for the workload (B for bursty, D balanced, E memory, F compute, L storage, M huge memory, N GPU) and the disk type for the I/O and SLA you need.
Inbound traffic needs an NSG rule; outbound traffic from new virtual networks needs an explicit method — a public IP, a NAT gateway or load balancer outbound rules.
Stopped is not deallocated: only deallocation stops the compute meter, and disks and public IPs are billed until deleted.

lab.title: Your first web server VM
lab.text:
What you'll build

Nusantara Retail's storefront gets its first home in Azure: an Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS virtual machine called vm-web-1 that runs nginx and serves a Nusantara Retail page to the internet. Traffic arrives through a Standard public IP and passes a network security group that allows only SSH and HTTP. Product images get their own 8 GiB data disk, mounted at /datadrive. You will resize the VM, schedule a daily auto-shutdown, and prove to the finance team which power state stops the compute bill.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)).
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/06-virtual-machines-basic
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 06)
VM=vm-web-1
echo "Resource group: $RG · region: $LOCATION · size: $VM_SIZE · image: $VM_IMAGE"

- This lab needs 2 vCPUs of regional quota. If you are not sure the size is offered to you, run bash ../common/check-environment.sh first.
- No setup.sh is needed: you build everything yourself.

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway.

Tip: Cloud Shell disconnects after about 20 minutes without input and forgets your variables. If that happens, cd back into the lab folder and run the source, RG=, VM= lines again — and IP= from Task 2.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–8 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Create the VM

One command creates the VM and every resource it depends on. You name each one so the resource group stays readable, and you choose a network range (10.20.0.0/16) that will never collide with head office's 10.0.0.0/16.

ensure_rg "$RG" 06

az vm create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name "$VM" \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --image "$VM_IMAGE" \
  --size "$VM_SIZE" \
  --admin-username "$ADMIN_USER" \
  --generate-ssh-keys \
  --vnet-name vnet-nusa-web --vnet-address-prefix 10.20.0.0/16 \
  --subnet snet-web --subnet-address-prefix 10.20.1.0/24 \
  --nsg nsg-web \
  --public-ip-address pip-web-1 --public-ip-sku Standard \
  --os-disk-name osdisk-web-1 --storage-sku StandardSSD_LRS \
  --output table

It takes one to three minutes. What the less obvious options do:

Option | Why
--image "$VM_IMAGE" | Ubuntu2404 is the CLI alias for Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (Gen2, so Trusted Launch is on by default)
--size "$VM_SIZE" | Standard_B2ats_v2: 2 burstable vCPUs and 1 GiB of memory — enough for nginx
--generate-ssh-keys | Creates ~/.ssh/id_rsa and ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub in Cloud Shell if they don't exist yet, and puts the public key on the VM. No password is set
--nsg nsg-web | Creates a network security group on the VM's NIC. For Linux the CLI adds one inbound rule: SSH (22) from anywhere
--public-ip-sku Standard | Basic public IPs are retired. A Standard IP is static and closed until an NSG allows traffic
--storage-sku StandardSSD_LRS | A Standard SSD OS disk keeps the lab cheap. Production would use Premium SSD (Lunch 06, section 3)

Now look at what was really created:

az resource list --resource-group "$RG" --query "[].{type:type, name:name}" --output table

Tip: Prefer the portal? Home › Virtual machines › Create › Azure virtual machine. On Basics: your resource group, name vm-web-1, your region, No infrastructure redundancy required, security type Trusted launch, image Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS – x64 Gen2, size Standard_B2ats_v2, authentication SSH public key with source Use existing public key (paste the output of cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub from Cloud Shell), username azureuser, inbound port SSH (22). On Disks: Standard SSD. On Networking: create a virtual network vnet-nusa-web (10.20.0.0/16) with subnet snet-web (10.20.1.0/24) and a new public IP. Then Review + create. The portal names some resources differently (for example vm-web-1-nsg); that's fine — the checks find them through the VM.

Checkpoint: the resource list shows six resources: a virtual machine, a disk, a network interface, a network security group, a public IP address and a virtual network (plus any VM extensions that your subscription's policies add automatically). Confirm the VM is running:

az vm show -d -g "$RG" -n "$VM" \
  --query "{power:powerState, size:hardwareProfile.vmSize, publicIp:publicIps, privateIp:privateIps}" -o table

Curious about the outbound change from the reading? Ask the subnet:

az network vnet subnet show -g "$RG" --vnet-name vnet-nusa-web -n snet-web --query defaultOutboundAccess -o tsv

false means a private subnet: no default outbound access. An empty result means the network was created with an older default. Either way your VM can reach the internet, because it has its own public IP — an explicit outbound method.

Task 2 · Connect with SSH from Cloud Shell

SSH is how you will administer this Linux server. Your private key is already in Cloud Shell, so there is nothing to type except yes the first time.

IP=$(az vm show -d -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query publicIps -o tsv)
echo "Public IP: $IP"
ssh "$ADMIN_USER@$IP"

Answer yes to the host-key question. You are now inside the VM. Look around, then leave:

uname -r                                   # the kernel Azure booted from the image
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MOUNTPOINTS        # disks the VM can see
curl -s -H Metadata:true "http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance/compute/vmSize?api-version=2021-02-01&format=text"; echo
exit

The curl command asks the Instance Metadata Service — a special address every Azure VM can reach — which size it is running on.

Checkpoint: your prompt changed to azureuser@vm-web-1 while connected; lsblk showed one disk of about 30 GB (the OS disk) and no temporary disk, because Basv2 sizes don't have one; the metadata service answered Standard_B2ats_v2.

Task 3 · Install nginx and publish the Nusantara Retail page

The VM downloads nginx from the Ubuntu package mirror. That works because its public IP gives it explicit outbound access. You can run commands over SSH without opening an interactive session:

ssh "$ADMIN_USER@$IP" 'sudo apt-get update -q && sudo DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y -q nginx'

Now copy the sample page from the lab folder and put it where nginx serves files from:

head -n 12 app/index.html                             # have a quick look first
scp app/index.html "$ADMIN_USER@$IP:index.html"
ssh "$ADMIN_USER@$IP" 'sudo cp ~/index.html /var/www/html/index.html && curl -s localhost | grep -o "<title>.*</title>"'

Finally, try the site from Cloud Shell — that is, from the internet:

curl -s -m 5 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$IP/"

Checkpoint: inside the VM, curl localhost printed <title>Nusantara Retail · Online Store</title>. From Cloud Shell you got 000 — the request timed out. nginx is working; something in front of it is not letting the shopper in. That is Task 4.

Task 4 · Open port 80

The NSG has a rule for SSH but none for HTTP, and its default rules deny everything else coming from the internet. az vm open-port adds an allow rule to the NSG on the VM's network interface.

az vm open-port -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --port 80 --priority 900 --output none

az network nsg rule list -g "$RG" --nsg-name nsg-web \
  --query "[].{name:name, priority:priority, port:destinationPortRange, source:sourceAddressPrefix, access:access}" -o table

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$IP/"

Open http://<your public IP> in a browser tab too.

Tip: Prefer the portal? vm-web-1 › Networking › Network settings › Create port rule › Inbound port rule, service HTTP, priority 900. The portal shows the effective rules on the same page — a handy way to see subnet and NIC rules together.

Checkpoint: the rule list shows the SSH rule (priority 1000) and a new rule for port 80 (priority 900). curl prints 200, and the browser shows the Nusantara Retail page.

Task 5 · Add and mount a data disk

Product images will grow; they don't belong on the OS disk. Attach a new 8 GiB Standard SSD at LUN 0 (the first data disk slot):

az vm disk attach -g "$RG" --vm-name "$VM" \
  --name disk-web-1-data --new --size-gb 8 --sku StandardSSD_LRS --lun 0 --output none

az vm show -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query "storageProfile.dataDisks[].{lun:lun, name:name, sizeGb:diskSizeGb}" -o table

Azure has attached the disk, but Linux sees only a raw, empty device. It still needs a partition, a filesystem and a mount point. The lab's mount-data-disk.sh does that, and you can run it through Run Command — no SSH, no open port, just the Azure VM agent:

az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts @mount-data-disk.sh --query "value[0].message" -o tsv

The script finds the disk at LUN 0, creates one GPT partition, formats it as ext4, mounts it at /datadrive, adds a line to /etc/fstab using the partition's UUID with the nofail option (so a missing disk never stops the VM from booting), and creates /datadrive/images. It is safe to run twice. Run Command takes 30–60 seconds.

Prefer to do it by hand over SSH?

ssh "$ADMIN_USER@$IP"
lsblk -o NAME,HCTL,SIZE,MOUNTPOINTS          # the new 8G disk has no partitions; the last HCTL number is the LUN
ls -l /dev/disk/azure/scsi1/ 2>/dev/null     # lun0 -> ../../../sdX on most images
DISK=/dev/sdc                                # <-- use the device you found!
sudo parted --script "$DISK" mklabel gpt mkpart primary ext4 0% 100%
sudo mkfs.ext4 -L datadrive "${DISK}1"
sudo mkdir -p /datadrive
echo "UUID=$(sudo blkid -s UUID -o value ${DISK}1) /datadrive ext4 defaults,nofail 0 2" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo mount /datadrive && df -h /datadrive
exit

Double-check the device name: formatting the wrong disk destroys its data.

Checkpoint: the Run Command output ends with a df line for /datadrive of about 8 GB. Confirm over SSH: ssh "$ADMIN_USER@$IP" 'df -h /datadrive && grep datadrive /etc/fstab'

Task 6 · Resize the VM

The Ramadan promotion is coming and Dewi wants more memory. Resizing is vertical scaling: same VM, different size, one restart. First see which sizes the VM's current hardware cluster offers with the same number of vCPUs:

az vm list-vm-resize-options -g "$RG" -n "$VM" \
  --query '[?numberOfCores==`2`].{size:name, memoryMb:memoryInMb}' -o table

Resize to Standard_B2als_v2 (2 vCPUs, 4 GiB) — or another 2-vCPU size from the list — and watch the site:

az vm resize -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --size Standard_B2als_v2 --output none
az vm show -d -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query "{size:hardwareProfile.vmSize, power:powerState, ip:publicIps}" -o table
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$IP/"

The free account's monthly VM hours cover Standard_B2ats_v2 but not the bigger size, so size back down when you are done:

az vm resize -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --size "$VM_SIZE" --output none

Checkpoint: after each resize the VM is running with the new size, the public IP is unchanged (Standard IPs are static) and the site answers 200 again. During each resize the site was briefly down — remember that when someone suggests resizing the production VM at noon.

Task 7 · Schedule auto-shutdown

The test copy of the storefront should not run all night. Auto-shutdown deallocates the VM at the same time every day. The CLI takes the time in UTC: 19:00 in Jakarta (UTC+7) is 1200. So that the VM doesn't switch itself off in the middle of this lab, schedule it three hours from now:

date -u +"It is now %H:%M UTC"
SHUTDOWN_UTC=$(date -u -d '+3 hours' +%H00)
az vm auto-shutdown -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --time "$SHUTDOWN_UTC" --output none
# Optional: add --email you@example.com to get a warning 30 minutes before each shutdown.

SCHED=$(az resource list -g "$RG" --resource-type Microsoft.DevTestLab/schedules --query "[0].name" -o tsv)
az resource show -g "$RG" --resource-type Microsoft.DevTestLab/schedules -n "$SCHED" \
  --query "{name:name, status:properties.status, time:properties.dailyRecurrence.time, timeZone:properties.timeZoneId}" -o table

Tip: Prefer the portal? vm-web-1 › Operations › Auto-shutdown: turn it on, pick a time, and choose the time zone (UTC+07:00) Bangkok, Hanoi, Jakarta so you never have to convert to UTC. You can add a notification email there.

Checkpoint: a schedule resource (type Microsoft.DevTestLab/schedules) exists in your resource group with status Enabled, your chosen time and time zone UTC.

Task 8 · Stopped versus deallocated

Finance asked whether they pay at night. Prove the answer. First stop the VM:

az vm stop -g "$RG" -n "$VM"
az vm show -d -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query powerState -o tsv

The power state says VM stopped: the operating system is off, but the VM is still allocated to its host, so the compute meter keeps running. Now deallocate it:

az vm deallocate -g "$RG" -n "$VM"
az vm get-instance-view -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query "instanceView.statuses[].displayStatus" -o tsv
az vm show -d -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query publicIps -o tsv

Then bring the shop back:

az vm start -g "$RG" -n "$VM"
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$IP/"
ssh "$ADMIN_USER@$IP" 'df -h /datadrive'

State you saw | Compute billed? | Disks billed? | Public IP
VM stopped | Yes | Yes | Kept
VM deallocated | No | Yes | Kept (Standard IPs are static) and billed

Checkpoint: you saw VM stopped, then VM deallocated, then VM running. The public IP never changed, the site answers 200, and /datadrive was mounted again automatically thanks to the fstab entry.

Break it and fix it

A colleague "tidied up" the NSG. Play the colleague — delete the rule that allows port 80:

RULE=$(az network nsg rule list -g "$RG" --nsg-name nsg-web --query "[?destinationPortRange=='80'].name | [0]" -o tsv)
echo "Deleting rule: $RULE"
az network nsg rule delete -g "$RG" --nsg-name nsg-web --name "$RULE"
curl -s -m 5 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$IP/"

Symptom: the shop is down — curl prints 000 after a five-second timeout, the browser spins, and bash verify.sh fails two checks. Yet nginx is fine: ssh "$ADMIN_USER@$IP" 'curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" localhost' prints 200. Find the cause and fix it without looking at the hint.

Hint and fix

The VM answers locally but not from the internet, and SSH still works — so the problem is between the internet and the VM, on port 80 only. List the rules (az network nsg rule list -g "$RG" --nsg-name nsg-web -o table): only SSH is allowed, and the default DenyAllInBound rule drops HTTP. Put the rule back:

az vm open-port -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --port 80 --priority 900 --output none
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$IP/"

Bonus: Azure Network Watcher can tell you which rule blocks a packet (Lunch 08 covers it): az network watcher test-ip-flow -g "$RG" --vm "$VM" --direction Inbound --protocol TCP --local "$(az vm show -d -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query privateIps -o tsv):80" --remote 203.0.113.10:50000

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. The data-disk mount check uses Run Command, so the script takes about a minute.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes everything the lab created (resource group rg-lunch06-<suffix>, including the VM, disks, public IP and the auto-shutdown schedule) and forgets the VM's host key in ~/.ssh/known_hosts. Your SSH key pair stays, because other labs reuse it. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
SkuNotAvailable … "The requested size for resource … is currently not available in location …" | The size isn't offered to your subscription in that region or zone | Run bash ../common/check-environment.sh, pick another 2-vCPU size, then export VM_SIZE=<size> and source ../common/config.sh again
"Operation could not be completed as it results in exceeding approved Total Regional Cores quota" | Other VMs already use your vCPU quota | Delete leftovers from other labs (bash ../common/check-environment.sh lists them) or request more quota
ssh: connect to host … port 22: Connection timed out | The VM is stopped/deallocated, or the SSH rule is missing | az vm start …; list the NSG rules and make sure port 22 is allowed
Permission denied (publickey) | Your Cloud Shell keys changed (for example an ephemeral session without storage) | Push your current key: az vm user update -g "$RG" -n "$VM" -u "$ADMIN_USER" --ssh-key-value "$(cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub)"
WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! | An earlier VM used the same public IP | ssh-keygen -R "$IP", then connect again
E: Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend | Ubuntu is still installing updates from the first boot | Wait two or three minutes and run the command again
curl prints 000 | No NSG rule for port 80, or the VM isn't running | Task 4; az vm show -d … --query powerState
curl prints 200 but you see "Welcome to nginx!" | The sample page wasn't copied | Repeat the scp and sudo cp lines in Task 3
Run Command fails with a conflict or "execution is in progress" | Another Run Command is still running on the VM | Wait a minute and run it again
mount-data-disk.sh says "No data disk found at LUN 0" | The disk isn't attached, or it was attached at another LUN | Check Task 5's dataDisks table; use --lun 0
Resize fails because the size is "not available in the current hardware cluster" | The cluster your VM runs on doesn't offer that size | az vm deallocate, then az vm resize, then az vm start
verify.sh says the VM is not running | Auto-shutdown fired, or you left it deallocated | az vm start -g "$RG" -n "$VM"

Stretch goals

- Lock SSH down. Allow port 22 only from your current Cloud Shell address (it can change between sessions): R22=$(az network nsg rule list -g "$RG" --nsg-name nsg-web --query "[?destinationPortRange=='22'].name | [0]" -o tsv) then az network nsg rule update -g "$RG" --nsg-name nsg-web -n "$R22" --source-address-prefixes "$(my_public_ip)/32".
- Serve images from the data disk. Over SSH: sudo ln -s /datadrive/images /var/www/html/images, copy a picture into /datadrive/images and open http://<IP>/images/<file>.
- Sign in with Microsoft Entra ID instead of a key. Give the VM a system-assigned identity (az vm identity assign -g "$RG" -n "$VM"), install the login extension (az vm extension set -g "$RG" --vm-name "$VM" --publisher Microsoft.Azure.ActiveDirectory --name AADSSHLoginForLinux), grant yourself Virtual Machine Administrator Login on the VM (az role assignment create --role "Virtual Machine Administrator Login" --assignee "$(my_upn)" --scope "$(az vm show -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query id -o tsv)"), then connect with az ssh vm -g "$RG" -n "$VM".
- Try Azure Bastion. In the portal, open vm-web-1 › Connect › Bastion. If your region offers the free Developer SKU you can connect from the browser — then remove the SSH rule entirely and see that Bastion still works.

Challenge brief

Build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep):

1. A resource group named rg-lunch06-<suffix> (rg_name 06) tagged course=azure-fundamentals-lunches and lunch=06 — ensure_rg "$RG" 06 does this for you.
2. A running Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS VM named vm-web-1, size $VM_SIZE, with SSH-key authentication only (no password) and a Standard public IP address.
3. An NSG on the VM's NIC or subnet that allows inbound TCP port 80 from the internet.
4. nginx serving a page that contains the text Nusantara Retail, returning HTTP 200 on http://<public IP>/.
5. At least one managed data disk attached to the VM, formatted and mounted at /datadrive so it survives a restart.
6. An enabled daily auto-shutdown schedule for the VM.
7. Not checked by the script, but do it: resize the VM and back, and observe stopped versus deallocated.

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode.
